texts.orig: Background: Pneumococcal conjugate vaccines (PCVs) are generally administered in infant schedules with other vaccines. Here, we describe the safety and immunogenicity of routinely recommended pediatric vaccines given with 20-valent-PCV (PCV20).
texts.text: Background: Pneumococcal conjugate vaccines (PCVs) are generally administered in infant schedules with other vaccines. Here, we describe the safety and immunogenicity of routinely recommended pediatric vaccines given with 20-valent-PCV (PCV20).

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Methods: Two phase 3, double-blind, randomized trials evaluated the safety, tolerability, and immunogenicity of PCV20 in infants with concomitant pediatric vaccines. The studies examined a 4-dose series (Study B7471011/ NCT04382326; N = 1997) and a 3-dose series (Study B7471012/NCT04546425; N = 1207). Concomitant vaccinations included a combination vaccine (diphtheria, tetanus, acellular pertussis [DTaP] with hepatitis B and poliovirus antigens (DTaP-HBV-IPV) and Haemophilus influenzae type b vaccine [Hib]) in Study B7471011 or combined vaccine (DTaP, hepatitis B, poliovirus, and Hib antigens [DTaP-HBV-IPV/Hib]) in Study B7471012. Measles, mumps, rubella (MMR) and varicella vaccines were given concomitantly with the toddler dose in both studies. Immunogenicity objectives were to demonstrate noninferiority of immune responses to concomitant vaccine antigens for concomitant vaccines given with PCV20 to those given with 13-valent PCV (PCV13). Safety endpoints included systemic events and adverse events (AEs).

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Results: Noninferiority was met for the primary objectives of percentage of participants with prespecified antibody levels to the DTaP-HBV-IPV and Hib 1 month after the third infant dose (Study B7471011) and 1 month after the toddler dose of DTaP-HBV-IPV/Hib (Study B7471012) in the PCV20 group compared with the PCV13 group. Noninferiority was also met for the geometric mean antibody levels to MMR and varicella vaccines 1 month after the toddler dose in both studies. Systemic event frequencies were similar in the PCV20 and PCV13 groups in both studies, with severity mostly reported as mild or moderate. Frequencies of reported AEs were similar between the PCV20 and PCV13 groups.

texts.orig: Conclusions: Immune responses to routine pediatric vaccines given with PCV20 were noninferior to those when given with PCV13. PCV20 may be safely administered with other routine pediatric vaccines. (NCT04382326; NCT04546425).

texts.orig: Pneumococcal disease is a significant cause of morbidity and mortality in children younger than 5 years and can lead to noninvasive conditions, such as acute otitis media, pneumonia, or life-threatening invasive pneumococcal disease (IPD), including bacteremia and bacterial meningitis [1 – 3]. Widespread implementation and uptake of pneumococcal conjugate vaccines (PCVs) through national infant immunization programs have substantially decreased the burden of pneumococcal disease worldwide [4 , 5].

texts.label: text
texts.orig: The first widely used PCV was 7-valent PCV (PCV7; serotypes 4, 6B, 9V, 14, 18C, 19F, 23F), which was licensed in 2000 and subsequently replaced with the 13-valent PCV (PCV13; 6 additional serotypes, 1, 3, 5, 6A, 7F, 19A) within infant immunization programs in 2010 [6 , 7]. Although uptake of PCVs averted an estimated 175 million global cases of pneumococcal disease and more than 620,000 associated deaths in children younger than 5 years, a substantial disease burden due to nonPCV13 serotypes has remained [4 , 8 – 11].

texts.label: text
texts.orig: To help address the need for expanded protection against additional serotypes, a 20-valent PCV (PCV20) containing PCV13 components and conjugates for 7 additional serotypes (8, 10A, 11A, 12F, 15B, 22F, 33F) was developed [12 – 19]. These additional serotypes were selected based on their global prevalence as a cause of pediatric pneumococcal disease and their association with increased disease severity, invasive potential, and antibiotic resistance [8 , 20 – 24]. PCV20 has been licensed in several countries for the prevention of pneumococcal pneumonia and IPD among adults ≥18 years of age, and for pediatric use from 6 weeks of age [25 – 30].

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Two key phase 3 infant immunogenicity and safety trials demonstrated that PCV20 elicited immune responses expected to protect infants against all vaccine serotypes and had a similar safety and tolerability profile to that of PCV13 [17 , 18]. Here, we expand on the findings from these studies on the immunogenicity and safety of routinely recommended pediatric vaccines administered concomitantly with PCV20.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: The study designs and ethical conduct of 2 phase 3, double-blind, randomized trials that evaluated the safety, tolerability, and immunogenicity of PCV20 in infants when administered concomitantly with routine childhood vaccines have been reported previously (Supplementary Fig. 1) [17 , 18]. Briefly, Study B7471011 (NCT04382326) evaluated 4 doses (3 infant doses plus a toddler dose) of PCV20, compared with PCV13, and enrolled 1997 participants from 92 sites in the United States and Puerto Rico from May 2020 to September 2022 [17]. Study B7471012 (NCT04546425) evaluated 3 doses (2 infant doses plus a toddler dose) of PCV20, compared with PCV13, and enrolled 1207 participants from 59 sites in Europe and Australia (primary analysis population) from September 2020 to April 2022 [18]. Participants were healthy infants born at >36 weeks of estimated gestational age who were approximately 2 months of age at the time of consent. Both studies excluded infants with previous receipt of the following vaccines: pneumococcal, diphtheria, tetanus, pertussis, poliomyelitis, or Haemophilus influenzae type b (Hib). Additional eligibility criteria and methodology have been previously reported [17 , 18].

texts.label: text
texts.orig: The primary concomitant immunogenicity objective for both studies was to demonstrate that immune responses elicited by specified concomitant vaccine antigens given with PCV20 were noninferior to immune responses elicited by concomitant vaccine antigens given with PCV13. In both studies, specified antigens were diphtheria toxoid, tetanus toxoid, pertussis antigens (filamentous hemagglutinin, pertactin, pertussis toxoid), hepatitis B surface antigen, poliovirus strains, and Hib. Responses were assessed at 1 month after Dose 3 (third infant dose) for DTaP, hepatitis B, poliovirus, and Hib antigens in Study B7471011 (4-dose series), and 1 month after Dose 3 (toddler dose) in Study B7471012 (3-dose series). Immune responses to MMR and varicella antigens were assessed after the toddler dose in both studies.

texts.orig: Participants were randomly selected for measurement and assessment of concomitant vaccine responses and included if they remained in the evaluable population, with the sample sizes of the subsets predetermined (varying by antigen) to ensure adequate power to show noninferiority for the specified analyses. Blood samples were collected at defined intervals (Supplementary Fig. 1), and antibody responses to concomitant vaccine antigens were measured using a validated multiplex Luminex immunoassay, chemiluminescent immunoassay, antibody microneutralization test, or immunoglobulin G enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay as appropriate for the concomitant vaccine antigen.

texts.orig: The overall safety results for PCV20 and PCV13 given in the setting of the concomitant pediatric vaccines specified for Study B7471011 and Study B7471012 have been fully reported previously [17 , 18]. PCV20 had a similar tolerability and safety profile as PCV13 in both studies, with mild to moderate reactogenicity and AEs generally consistent with illnesses and medical conditions expected in infant and toddler populations [17 , 18]. There were no SAEs considered by the investigator to be related to PCV20 in Study B7471011 [17]. In Study B7471012, a previously reported SAE of inflammation 7 days after Dose 1 of PCV20 was considered by the investigator to be potentially related to PCV20 or DTaP-HBV-IPV/Hib combination vaccine [18].

texts.orig: Guidance on routine pediatric immunizations advises administration of multiple vaccines concomitantly to enhance vaccine uptake and compliance, as well as reduce burden on both healthcare systems and individuals [31]. Incorporation of PCV20 into infant immunization programs has the potential to expand protection for children against PCV serotypes by protecting against additional serotypes while also maintaining established protection against disease from PCV13 serotypes. Importantly, the clinical development program for PCV20 included assessment of safety and immunogenicity of routine concomitant pediatric vaccines.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Findings from these trials can potentially reflect real-world use of PCV20 and incorporation into routine vaccination schedules for infants. This analysis does not differentiate between systemic events and AEs arising from either PCV20 or PCV13 compared with concomitant vaccines, potentially confounding severity responses across vaccines. However, it would not be feasible or ethical to delay vaccination or include a control group without a PCV. Moreover, the study design reflects real-world scenarios wherein infants receive multiple pediatric vaccinations simultaneously, demonstrating that most events were mild to moderate when PCV20 was administered with concomitant pediatric vaccines. Additionally, subgroup safety data are described for participants receiving concomitant influenza and rotavirus vaccines. These were assessed retrospectively in nonrandomized populations with unequal sample sizes and were exploratory in nature; conclusions arising from these exploratory data should be interpreted with caution. Finally, it is worth noting that the 2 randomized trials were not powered to detect and attribute rarer adverse events. Ongoing surveillance and realworld studies will continue to monitor safety.
